Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 84, verses 1–4:

﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾. Scholars differ over this splitting: is it the sky being rent by clouds, or its opening up into gates? The answer to "when" (idhā) is omitted, to make it more awe-inspiring, since the listener will imagine the utmost of what he can conceive. It is omitted because it is known, being satisfied with the answer given in Surat al-Takwir and Surat al-Infitar. It has also been said that the answer is what is indicated by ﴿fa-mulāqīhi﴾ (﴿so you will meet it﴾), meaning: when the sky splits asunder, man will meet his Lord. It has also been said that the answer is ﴿adhinat﴾ (﴿it has listened﴾), with the waw added, but this view is weak.

﴿And it has listened to its Lord﴾. The linguistic meaning of adhinat is "it listened," and it is an expression for its obedience to its Lord, and that it submitted to God when He willed its splitting. Likewise is the obedience of the earth when He wills its stretching out and casting forth what is within it.

﴿And has been made to obey﴾. That is, it is right for it to listen and obey its Lord, or it is right for it to be split apart by the terrors of the Resurrection. This word comes from the saying: "He is worthy (ḥaqīq) of such-and-such," or "he is due it (maḥqūq bihi)," meaning: it is incumbent upon him to do it. So the meaning is: it is incumbent upon the sky to listen and obey its Lord, or it is incumbent upon it to be split. It is possible that the original form was ḥaqqat, with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and a ḍamma on the qāf, in the sense of wonder; then the first qāf was assimilated into the following qāf and its vowel was transferred to the ḥā'.

﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾. That is, what is upon it of mountains disappears until it becomes level.

﴿And casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾. That is, it casts out what is in its belly of the dead for the gathering. It has also been said: it casts out the treasures within it. This view is weak, because that happens at the time of the emergence of the Dajjal before the Resurrection, whereas the intended subject is the Day of Resurrection. And "takhallat" means: it remains empty of what was in it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 84, verses 6–9:

﴿O mankind﴾: an address to the whole human species. ﴿Indeed, you are laboring (kadih) toward your Lord﴾. Kadh (exertion, a term meaning striving, diligence and haste) in the language means: earnestness, striving and speed. The meaning is that you are exerting utmost effort in journeying toward your Lord, because time flies, and every moment you are cutting off a portion of your short life. It is as if you are a traveler hastening toward death, and then you will meet your Lord. It was also said: the meaning is that you are diligent in what you do, whether good or evil, and then you will meet your Lord, who will recompense you for it. The first interpretation is more apparent, because kadih is followed by ilá (toward) since it includes the meaning of journeying. Had it meant "working," it would have said: "for your Lord."

﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will be given an easy account, and he will return to his people, joyful.﴾ This is mentioned in Surah al-Haqqah: ﴿Then he will be called to account with an easy account﴾. The word yasir (easy) may mean "few," or it may mean "light and simple."

In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is subjected to a thorough reckoning will be punished." Then ʿĀ'ishah said: "Did Allah not say: ﴿he will be given an easy account﴾?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is only the presentation (ʿardh). As for whoever is subjected to a thorough reckoning, he will be ruined."

Also, a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): that Allah will bring the servant near on the Day of Resurrection until He places His covering (kanaf) over him, then says: "Did you do such and such?" and enumerates his sins to him. Then He says: "I concealed them from you in the world, and today I forgive them for you."

It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes account of himself in this world, Allah will make his reckoning light on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿and he will return to his people, joyful﴾: that is, he will return to his people in Paradise, joyful with what Allah has given him. The "people" (ahl) are his wives in Paradise, from the women of this world or from the ḥūr ʿīn (wide-eyed maidens). It may also mean his relatives among the believers, and Zamakhsharī interpreted it in this way.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 84, verses 10–15:

﴿But as for him who is given his record behind his back﴾: he means the disbeliever. It is related that these two verses were revealed concerning Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad, who was among the excellent believers, and concerning his brother Aswad, who was among the stubborn disbelievers, though their wording is more general than that. If it is said: How does He say here that the disbeliever is given his record behind his back, while in al-Haqqah He says [he takes it] with his left hand? The answer has two aspects. The first is that his hands will be shackled to his neck, and his left hand will be brought behind his back, so he takes his record with it. It is also said: his left hand will be made to enter his chest and come out from his back, so he takes his record with it. ﴿He will cry out for destruction﴾: that is, he will shout out "woe" and "perdition." ﴿Indeed, he was among his people, happy﴾: that is, in the world he was joyful among his family, enjoying comfort and heedless of the Hereafter. This stands in contrast to what is mentioned about the believer, that he returns to his family joyful in Paradise, and it is the opposite of what is related of the believers in Paradise when they say: "Indeed, we were before this among our people, fearful." ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return﴾: that is, he would not return to Allah. The meaning is that he denies the Resurrection. ﴿Yes [indeed]﴾: that is, he will return and be resurrected.

﴿So I swear﴾ — mentioned in its parallels — ﴿by the twilight﴾: it is the redness that remains after the sun sets. Abu Hanifa said it is the whiteness. It was also said that it is the whole day. This is weak, and the first view is the one known to the jurists (fuqaha') and to the lexicographers (ahl al-lugha). ﴿And the night and what it gathers﴾: that is, what it collects and gathers together. From this comes the word wasq (a load or measure). That night gathers things together and covers them with its darkness. ﴿And the moon when it becomes full﴾: that is, when it is complete on the fourteenth night. The form of ittasaq is ifta'ala, and it is derived from wasq, as if it has been filled with light. In this verse there is one of the devices of eloquence called luzum ma la yalzam (the obligation of what is not obligatory), due to the consistent use of the sin before the qaf in wasaq and ittasaq.

﴿You will surely embark stage after stage﴾: the word tabaq in the language has two meanings. The first: what matches another thing. One says, "this is tabaq for this" when it matches it. On the second meaning, the sense is: you will surely pass through states after states, which are layers one upon another. Then the scholars differed in interpreting these states. In the reading tarkabunna with a damma on the ba' (turkabunna), it is addressed to the human race. On this reading there are three views regarding the interpretation of the states: the first is that they are the hardships of death, then resurrection, then reckoning, then recompense. The second is that they are the human being's condition from a drop (nutfah), then a clot ( 'alaqah), until he comes out into this world, then until he grows old and then dies. As for the one who reads tarkabanna with a fatha on the ba', it is addressed to the human being according to the three meanings we mentioned. It was also said that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Those who hold this view then differed into three views. The first: you will surely endure the struggle with the disbelievers state after state. The second: you will surely conquer the lands one after another. The third: you will surely ascend through the heavens on the Night Journey (al-Isra'), one heaven after another. The phrase ﴿from stage﴾ ('an tabaq) is either in the position of a qualifier for tabaqan, or in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in tarkabunna. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 84, verse 20–25:

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the meaning is: what prevents them from believing?

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate?﴾ This is a place of prostration according to al-Shafi'i and others, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated in it. According to Malik, it is not among the obligatory prostrations (ʿazaʾim al-sajdat).

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ means the ones previously mentioned. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to describe them with disbelief.

﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal﴾ meaning: of what they gather in their breasts of disbelief and denial, or of what they gather in their records. It is said: "awʿaytu al-mal wa ghayrihi" when one gathers wealth or other things.

﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ The word "tidings" (bashshir) has been placed in the position of warning (nadhdhir), as a mockery of them.

﴿Except those who believe﴾ meaning: those among these disbelievers for whom belief has been decreed. On this interpretation the exception is contiguous (muttasil), and Ibn ʿAtiyya indicated this view. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is disjunctive (munqatiʿ).

﴿For them is a reward never to be cut off﴾ This has already been mentioned.
